title: Compounded GLP-1 Weight-Loss Injections Recalled Nationwide Over Sterility Concerns — Including Vials From a Houston Pharmacy
excerpt: The FDA has classified nationwide recalls of compounded tirzepatide injections — the GLP-1 drug sold under the brand names Mounjaro and Zepbound — as Class II after sterility could not be assured, including 64 vials recalled by a Houston pharmacy.
content:
Compounded GLP-1 weight-loss injections are being recalled nationwide because their sterility cannot be assured, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Apothecary Pharma LLC, a compounding pharmacy based in Cary, North Carolina, voluntarily recalled 22 vials of compounded tirzepatide and one vial of NAD+ injection distributed across the United States, USA TODAY reported.

Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in the FDA-approved brand-name drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound. The recalled products are compounded versions — custom formulations made by a specialized pharmacy — and are not FDA-approved finished drug products. The recall began Sept. 24 over a “lack of assurance of sterility,” and the FDA classified it as a Class II recall in October, according to Fox Business. A Class II classification means using the product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, while the likelihood of serious harm is considered small.

The affected tirzepatide is an 18 mg/mL prescription injection in a 4 mL multidose vial, covering lots AP-202622 through AP-202625 and AP-202627 through AP-202644, with beyond-use dates from Oct. 7 through Nov. 26, 2026, according to the FDA notice cited by Fox Business. The recalled NAD+ injection lot is AP-202647, with a beyond-use date of Oct. 13, 2026. The pharmacy notified recipients by letter, and the recall remains ongoing.

A Houston pharmacy is on the list, too

The recalls reach Texas directly. Houston RX, a Houston compounding pharmacy, recalled 64 vials of compounded tirzepatide-niacinamide and seven vials of compounded sermorelin, also classified as Class II recalls, after an August FDA inspection produced a Form 483 listing 14 observations, according to Medical Daily. Inspectors reported findings that included exposed skin during sterile work, reversed cleanroom air pressure, microbial growth in a clean hood, unsterilized equipment, possible mold near the cleanroom and research-grade ingredients. No illnesses linked to the recalled vials have been publicly reported.

A pharmacy the FDA had already warned

The Apothecary Pharma recall follows a December 2025 FDA warning letter that cited “serious deficiencies” in the company’s practices for producing drugs intended to be sterile, which the agency said put patients at risk, according to USA TODAY. The letter followed a May 2025 inspection of the company’s North Carolina facility. The FDA has not established a connection between those findings and the current recall.

Compounded GLP-1 drugs have been a special focus of the FDA since tirzepatide and semaglutide were removed from the official drug shortage list in late 2024 and early 2025, USA TODAY reported. Compounding pharmacies that had filled the gap for millions of patients were expected to stop producing the drugs en masse; many continued, prompting agency warnings and legal challenges.
